subtype: Approach: step away with support and a safe exit plan [Revision]
passage: In a rented room in Leeds, Siddiq read the message again: "Come alone tomorrow, the leader wants a private word." His stomach tightened. For weeks the evening meetings had felt friendly, but the private talks had begun asking for his passport "for safekeeping". He called Valentina, a friend from his course. "I want to stop going. Will you be at my flat at six?" She said yes and told him to ring his parents as well. The next day he did not go. Two members waited outside his building, and Valentina and a flatmate stayed at his side until they left. He wrote to the group that he would not be back and saved every message. His parents told him that if anyone threatened him he should call the police.

qa.q: What had the private talks begun asking for?
qa.a: The private talks had begun asking for his passport for safekeeping.

qa.q: How was Siddiq feeling when he read the message?
qa.a: Siddiq felt uneasy and anxious, and his stomach tightened.

qa.q: What else could Siddiq do, and why?
qa.a: Siddiq could tell a course tutor or the university welfare team and go to the police if threats came, because more people who know make the exit safer.

qa.q: How might Valentina have seen the situation?
qa.a: Valentina was probably worried but glad to be trusted, and ready to stay by his side.

grounding: Illustrates stepping away from a group by telling a trusted friend, avoiding private meetings and leaning on family with the police as a fallback.

subtype: Approach: step away with support and a safe exit plan [Revision]
passage:
The college counselling centre was quiet at four. Vaibhav sat across from the counsellor with his friend Leela beside him, which was the first step he'd planned.
"I've been going to this group for two months," he said. "Lately they want me at meetings alone with the leader. When I said I wanted to take a break, he said I'd 'regret betraying the family'."
The counsellor listened. "What are you thinking of doing?"
Vaibhav had written it down. "I've told Leela everything. I won't meet anyone from the group alone. I'll stop going from this week. I've told my parents; they're driving down on Saturday. And if anyone threatens me, I'll go to the police."
"That's a good plan," the counsellor said. "Let's add one thing: if anyone from the group turns up at the hostel, tell the warden straight away." The counsellor called the hostel warden while they were still in the room.
Leela squeezed his arm on the way out.

qa.q: Who did Vaibhav bring to the counselling centre?
How was Vaibhav feeling about the leader's words?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and pressured, especially by private meetings and being told he would regret betraying the family.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do to stay safe in the weeks after leaving?
qa.a: He could keep Leela and the warden informed of any contact from the group and save any threatening messages for the police.

qa.q: How does the plan look to the counsellor?
qa.a: The counsellor sees it as a good, careful plan and strengthens it by adding the warden and calling the warden at once.

grounding: Shows the person stepping away from a group with a trusted friend, no private meetings, family support and police if threatened, with the college acting too.

subtype: Approach: step away with support and a safe exit plan [Revision]
passage:
Himani,
I'm writing because you asked why I stopped going to the Sunday group. I didn't want to explain in the canteen.
It started feeling wrong in March. The leader began asking me to stay after sessions to talk alone. He said I was "special" and shouldn't tell my family about our talks. My stomach turned every time.
So I made a plan and didn't do it alone. First I told my friend Tenzin everything. Then I stopped meeting anyone from the group without someone else present. I called my parents; Papa came that weekend and stayed two days. I simply stopped going.
Two members kept messaging, saying I'd "regret leaving". When one wrote that they knew where my hostel was, Papa and I went to the police station and showed them the messages. The officer noted it and called the member. The messages stopped.
If you ever feel that twist in your stomach there, tell me.
Leela

qa.q: Who did Leela tell first about the group?
qa.a: Leela told her friend Tenzin everything first.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the leader asked for private talks?
qa.a: Leela felt uneasy and frightened, with a stomach that turned every time.

qa.q: What else could Himani do if she starts feeling uneasy in the group?
qa.a: Himani could tell Leela or a family member, avoid being alone with leaders, and step away with someone's support.

qa.q: How might Leela's father have felt when he saw the messages?
qa.a: Papa likely felt protective and worried, which is why he went with Leela to the police station.

grounding: Shows the person, feeling uneasy, telling a trusted friend, avoiding private meetings with the leader, stopping attending and going to the police when threatened.
